train_texts: Case originated in an application (no. 68250/11) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the decision of the Cologne Court of Appeal of [DATE_TIME] not to stay the execution of the detention order against him breached Article 5 of the Convention. The Turkish Government, having been informed of their right to intervene in the proceedings, did not make use of this right. The remainder of the application was declared inadmissible pursuant to Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court. The case was decided in favour of the applicant, who had been granted legal aid. The applicant was convicted of three counts of commercial trafficking in a substantial amount of drugs. He was also charged with two counts of unlawful possession of a weapon. The court sentenced him to two years in prison, but the applicant appealed the sentence. He argued there was no incentive for him to abscond, as he lived with his parents and had two children. The appeals court agreed. The case was referred to the Aachen Regional Court for further proceedings. The trial was adjourned until January 15, when the trial was set to start again. The applicant was released on bail on the condition that he paid back the money he had borrowed. Aachen Regional Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal. He then lodged a further appeal against that decision. The applicant proposed that his family furnish security of EUR 10,000. The family was, however, unwilling to put the money at the applicant's disposal as they were unwilling to run the risk of having the repayment claim attached for payment against future claims the authorities might have against the applicant. The court asked the applicant to clarify the offer made and requested that the necessary means be given to him by his family in a manner that allowed him to dispose freely of those means and to furnish the security himself. The lawful origin of those Means had to be credibly demonstrated. The Cologne Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s further appeal. It endorsed the assessments of the District Court and the Regional Court as to the risk of the applicant's absconding. The decision was served on the applicant on [DATE_TIME]. On the same day, the Aachen District Court stayed the execution of the detention order against the applicant. Upon the furnishing of EUR 5,000 by another person by the applicant, the applicant was released from detention. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to accept the applicant ‘s constitutional complaint’ against the decision not to stay the execution of the detention order against him.

They were unwilling to run the risk of having the repayment claim attached for payment against future claims the authorities might have against the applicant. Cologne Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s further appeal. Aachen District Court stayed the execution of the detention order against the applicant on a number of conditions, including that he or another person furnish security of EUR 5,000. Upon the furnishing of that amount by another person that same day, the applicant was released from detention. The Federal Constitutional Court declined to accept the applicant's constitutional complaint against the Court of appeal's decision. The decision was served on the applicant. on [DATE_TIME]. PROCEDURE

The case originated in an application (no. 68250/11) against [LOCATION] lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a [NRP] national, Mr [PERSON] (“the applicant”), on [DATE_TIME].

The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by [PERSON], a lawyer practising in [LOCATION]. The German Government (“the Government”) were represented by one of their Agents, Mr [PERSON], [LOCATION], of the Federal Ministry of Justice and Consumer Protection.

The applicant alleged, in particular, that the decision of the Cologne Court of Appeal of [DATE_TIME] not to stay the execution of the detention order against him breached Article 5 § 4 of the Convention.

On [DATE_TIME] the complaint concerning Article 5 § 4 of the Convention was communicated to the Government and the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible pursuant to Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court.

The Turkish Government, having been informed of their right to intervene in the proceedings (Article 36 § 1 of the Convention and Rule 44 of the Rules of Court), did not make use of this right.

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

The applicant was born in [DATE_TIME] and lives in [LOCATION].

On [DATE_TIME] the premises in which the applicant ran a café were searched, based on a search warrant of [DATE_TIME] issued by the Aachen District Court. The applicant was found in a back room of the café, weighing and packaging some 400 grams of cocaine, with a sum of 2,325 euros (EUR) in the pockets of his trousers. He was arrested.

The following day, the Aachen District Court issued a warrant for the arrest of the applicant on the ground that he was strongly suspected ([PERSON]) of commercial trafficking of a substantial amount of drugs and that there was a risk of his absconding. It considered that the applicant could face a considerable prison sentence for the offences in question, that he did not have strong ties to [LOCATION], that he was unemployed and living on social security, and that he could easily abscond to [LOCATION].

At a detention review hearing on [DATE_TIME], the applicant’s counsel applied for the applicant’s release on bail, stating that the applicant’s family were able and willing to furnish the amount of bail to be determined by the court. [DATE_TIME], the applicant’s counsel withdrew the application after the court indicated that bail would not be granted.

On [DATE_TIME] the Public Prosecutor’s Office lodged a bill of indictment against the applicant, charging him with three counts of commercial trafficking of a substantial amount of drugs.

On [DATE_TIME] the Aachen District Court decided to open the trial against the applicant.

On [DATE_TIME] the District Court convicted the applicant on one of three counts of commercial trafficking in a substantial amount of drugs and acquitted him on the other two counts. It sentenced him to [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME] imprisonment and ordered the continuation of his detention.

On [DATE_TIME] both the applicant and the Public Prosecutor lodged appeals against the District Court’s judgment.

That same day, the applicant lodged an appeal against the decision ordering his continued detention and asked for the detention order to be set aside or its execution to be stayed. He argued that there was no incentive for him to abscond. The strength of his ties to [LOCATION] rendered his absconding to [LOCATION] unlikely. He had lived in [LOCATION] for [DATE_TIME], had been married for [DATE_TIME], and had two children, aged [DATE_TIME]. His parents and his brother also lived in [LOCATION]. His only tie to [LOCATION], by contrast, was his parents’ holiday home.

On [DATE_TIME] the Aachen District Court decided not to grant the applicant’s appeal against the continued detention order and to refer the matter to the Aachen Regional Court. It considered that it was possible that the applicant would be sentenced to a significant prison sentence on appeal. There was, hence, an incentive for him to abscond which was not counterbalanced by his existing social ties to [LOCATION]. In that regard, it noted that the applicant and his entire family had lived on social security since [DATE_TIME], that his command of the [NRP] language was insufficient and that he had no prospects of employment. Considering that his wife was also a [NRP] national, that his children were of a young age and that his parents owned a holiday home in [LOCATION], there was a risk that the applicant would abscond to [LOCATION] with his family. This risk could not be adequately remedied by reporting requirements or payment of security.

On [DATE_TIME] the Aachen Regional Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal. It limited the basis of the detention order to the count on which he had been convicted and annulled it for the two counts on which he had been acquitted by the District Court. Yet, referring to the reasoning of the District Court and underlining that the applicant had no legal employment whereas he had family ties to [LOCATION], it considered that there continued to be a risk of the applicant’s absconding.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant lodged a further appeal against that decision. After essentially reiterating his earlier submission as to why there was no risk of his absconding, he stated that such risk could, in any event, be remedied by imposing a less severe measure. In that regard, he proposed that his family furnish security of EUR 10,000.

After the Regional Court decided not to grant the applicant’s further appeal and to refer the matter to the Cologne Court of Appeal, that court informed the applicant’s counsel, in a letter dated [DATE_TIME], that it was considering staying the execution of the detention order. It asked the applicant to clarify the offer made and requested that the necessary means be given to him by his family in a manner that allowed him to dispose freely of those means and to furnish the security himself. The lawful origin of those means had to be credibly demonstrated.

[DATE_TIME], the applicant’s counsel informed the Court of Appeal that the applicant’s family was able and willing to furnish security of EUR 10,000 to the court and to demonstrate credibly the lawful origin of those means. The family was, however, unwilling to put the money at the applicant’s disposal as they were unwilling to run the risk of having the repayment claim attached for payment against future claims the authorities might have against the applicant. He added that, if the applicant had to assume that the security would be forfeited in any event, that is to say, even if he did not abscond, because the repayment claim would be attached for payment against other claims, the security could not effectively remedy a risk of his absconding.

On [DATE_TIME] the Cologne Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s further appeal. It endorsed the assessments of the District Court and the Regional Court as to the risk of the applicant’s absconding and noted that the sentence the applicant risked incurring was not limited to [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME] imprisonment, for the Public Prosecutor had appealed against the District Court’s judgment, seeking the applicant’s conviction on the two counts on which he had been acquitted. It stated that it would nonetheless consider staying the execution of the detention order if security were furnished. As long as the applicant’s family was not willing to put the necessary means at his own disposal it was, however, not ready to do so, arguing that this unwillingness indicated that his family lacked confidence in him and concluding that the family ties appeared not to be strong enough to prevent him from risking forfeiture of the security by absconding. The Court of Appeal furthermore found that there was a risk that the applicant would commit more drug-related offences if he were released from detention and also based the detention order, by way of subsidiarity, on a risk of reoffending. The decision was served on the applicant on [DATE_TIME].

On [DATE_TIME] the District Court’s judgment of [DATE_TIME] became final, following the Regional Court’s decision to discontinue the proceedings in relation to one of the charges and the withdrawal of appeals by both the applicant and the Public Prosecutor.

That same day, the Aachen District Court stayed the execution of the detention order against the applicant on a number of conditions, including that either he or another person furnish security of EUR 5,000. Upon the furnishing of that amount by another person that same day, the applicant was released from detention.

On [DATE_TIME] the Federal Constitutional Court declined to accept the applicant’s constitutional complaint against the Court of Appeal’s decision not to stay the execution of the detention order against him, lodged on [DATE_TIME], for adjudication, without providing reasons (file no. 2 BvR 155/11).

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 48539/99) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant complained of the use of covert audio and video surveillance within his cell, the prison visiting area and upon a fellow prisoner. He relied on Articles 6, [DATE_TIME] and 13 of the convention. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court. The parties replied in writing to each other's observations. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). An anonymous informant told the police that the applicant had been involved in the murder of [PERSON]. On [DATE_TIME] Detective Chief Inspector requested permission for the cell and the visiting areas used by the applicant and [P PERSON] to be bugged with audio and video technology. The Chief Constable of the Greater Manchester Police granted authority for an unlimited period for both the police stations at [LOCATION] and [CAMPAIGN] The applicant was held for long periods in the same cell and recordings of their conversations were made. The applicant and his female friend were recorded on audio and videotape in the prison visiting area. The police told the applicant that he was not obliged to say anything.  applicant was taken away from the prison to be interviewed by the police concerning the Kwik-Save robbery. He was attended and advised by his solicitor. The recording thereby obtained was adduced in evidence at the applicant's trial. The judge concluded that there was evidence on the tapes from which the jury could infer that the applicant was involved in the events of [DATE_TIME], and it was not so unreliable that it could not be left to the jury to assess for themselves. No evidence, other than the alleged admissions, connected the applicant with the killing of Mr [PERSON]. The applicant was convicted of murder and a count of conspiracy to rob. The judge's ruling on the admissibility of the evidence was given on [DATE_TIME), after a voir dire (submissions on a point of law in the absence of a jury) and consisted of a judgment of eighteen pages. He considered that the use of an informant to talk and listen to the accused over a substantial period of time did not result in any unfairness. The fact that [PERSON] might be considered as having much to gain in giving evidence was also a matter to be left to the jury in their assessment of the reliability of his evidence. The evidence was accordingly admitted before the jury. The judge also directed the jury concerning the possible drawing of inferences from the applicant's silence in police interview on 28 and [DATE_TIME] The judge told the jury that the defence had contended that the applicant’s silence had been adopted on legal advice because of the view that oppressive interrogation techniques were being used. The applicant thereafter lodged a notice of appeal, asserting, inter alia, that the judge ought to have excluded evidence of the audio- and video-recordings of his conversations with [PERSON] and J.N.S. and the evidence put forward by [Person] He was refused leave to appeal against his conviction by a single judge. Lord Justice [PERSON] found that the trial judge gave a very careful and impeccable ruling as regards the admissibility of the tapes and evidence. There was no basis for holding that the exercise of his discretion had been so flawed that the Court of Appeal should intervene. The judge had given an entirely appropriate direction to the jury in the circumstances of the case. The applicant complained that the judge should have warned the jury not to take into account the applicant's failure to answer police questioning in the light of the police strategy to “spook” him. PROCEDURE

The case originated in an application (no. 48539/99) against [LOCATION] [LOCATION] and [LOCATION] lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a [LOCATION] national, Mr [PERSON] (“the applicant”), on [DATE_TIME].

The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented before the Court by Mr [PERSON], a lawyer practising in [LOCATION]. The United Kingdom Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr [PERSON], of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office.

The applicant complained of the use of covert audio and video surveillance within his cell, the prison visiting area and upon a fellow prisoner and of the use of materials gained by these means at his trial for murder. He relied on Articles 6, [DATE_TIME] and 13 of the Convention.

The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1.

By a decision of [DATE_TIME], the Chamber declared the application partly admissible.

On [DATE_TIME] the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section (Rule 52 § 1).

The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). The parties replied in writing to each other's observations.

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

On [DATE_TIME] Mr [PERSON], store manager, was shot dead in the manager's office of a Kwik-Save supermarket in [LOCATION].

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant and another man, by the name of [PERSON], were arrested on suspicion of having committed a robbery at the Late Saver shop, Cheadle. At the time, they were in possession of an 8-mm Beretta replica handgun. Charged in connection with this offence, Mr [PERSON] admitted to the offence and several other [DATE_TIME] shop robberies. The applicant denied involvement in any of the offences. On or [DATE_TIME] an anonymous informant told the police that the applicant had been involved in the murder of [PERSON].

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant and [PERSON] appeared in custody at the Stockport Magistrates' Court and were further remanded in custody to reappear on [DATE_TIME]. On [DATE_TIME] Detective Chief Inspector [PERSON] requested permission for the cell and the visiting areas used by the applicant and [PERSON] to be bugged with audio and video technology, alleging that all regular methods of investigation to identify [PERSON] murderer had failed. The Chief Constable of the Greater Manchester Police granted authority on [DATE_TIME] for an unlimited period for both the police stations at [LOCATION] and [PERSON]. On [DATE_TIME] similar authority was sought and obtained for the installation of a listening device with video system to be placed in the visiting area of [LOCATION] police station, where the applicant was then held.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant was arrested for the murder and questioned. In the interviews with the police which followed, the police told the applicant that he was not obliged to say anything. He availed himself of that right.

During this time visits to the applicant by his female friend, [PERSON], were recorded on audio and videotape in the prison visiting area [DATE_TIME]. The applicant and [PERSON] were held for long periods in the same cell and recordings of their conversations were made from [DATE_TIME].

On [DATE_TIME] H. was brought to [LOCATION] police station. H. was a long-standing police informant with a criminal record who had been arrested on [DATE_TIME] for unrelated offences. He was placed in the applicant's cell for the purpose of eliciting information from the applicant. As asserted by the applicant, [PERSON] had every incentive to inform on him. Telephone conversations between [PERSON] and the police included comments by the police instructing H. to “push him for what you can” and disclosed evidence of concerted police coaching. After [DATE_TIME] he associated regularly with the applicant who was remanded at Strangeways Prison.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant was taken away from the prison to be interviewed by the police concerning the Kwik-Save robbery. He was attended and advised by his solicitor. During the course of the interview, the applicant was invited to comment on the recordings made in [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME]. He made no comment to any question. According to the applicant, he was interrogated at length by the police in an attempt to “rattle” or unsettle him, such that he would be more talkative and vulnerable to [PERSON] upon his return to the prison. H. had been fitted with recording devices. The recording thereby obtained was adduced in evidence at the applicant's trial.

The applicant was interviewed again in the presence of his solicitor on [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME] and remained silent when faced with the allegations.

On [DATE_TIME] H. made a 59- to 60-page witness statement detailing his conversations with the applicant and was released on bail on [DATE_TIME]. His sentence was postponed until after he had given evidence at the applicant's trial. The high point of H.'s evidence was the assertion that the applicant had admitted his presence at the murder scene. This asserted admission was not part of the recorded interview and was disputed. The thrust of the applicant's case was that he was discussing robberies and did not accede to H.'s efforts to channel their conversation into a discussion of the murder. The audio- and video-recordings (or transcripts thereof) were utilised in the trial of the applicant. No evidence, other than the alleged admissions, connected the applicant with the killing of Mr [PERSON].

In [DATE_TIME] the applicant's trial on one count of murder and a count of conspiracy to rob began before a jury. He was represented by leading counsel.

During his trial, the applicant's counsel challenged the admissibility of extracts from covert audio- and video-recordings of conversations of the applicant with [PERSON] and J.N.S., under sections 76 and 78 of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act [DATE_TIME] (PACE). The judge concluded that there was evidence on the tapes from which the jury could infer that the applicant was involved in the events of [DATE_TIME], and it was not so unreliable that it could not be left to the jury to assess for themselves. The judge also rejected the applicant's counsel's arguments under sections 76 and 78 of PACE that the evidence from [PERSON] was obtained by oppression or by such impropriety as to render it inadmissible. He considered that the use of an informant to talk and listen to the accused over a substantial period of time did not result in any unfairness to the accused. The fact that [PERSON] might be considered as having much to gain in giving evidence was also a matter to be left to the jury in their assessment of the reliability of his evidence. The evidence was accordingly admitted before the jury. The judge's ruling on the admissibility of the evidence was given on [DATE_TIME], after a voir dire (submissions on a point of law in the absence of a jury) and consisted of a judgment of eighteen pages.

In his summing-up to the jury on [DATE_TIME], the trial judge gave directions on the way in which the jury should assess the reliability of the disputed evidence. He told them that they were to judge whether the police had deliberately wound up the applicant during the interview on [DATE_TIME] and how to approach the evidence put forward by [PERSON]: “So at [DATE_TIME] with regard to H. you have his evidence about the conversations that he had with [the applicant] and what [the applicant] said. You have the tape recordings of the conversations on [DATE_TIME] when H. had been wired up, between [the applicant] and [PERSON], and you have the transcripts of the conversations between [PERSON] and the police. I suggest ... that you approach the evidence of [PERSON] with the very greatest caution and care. He is a professional criminal. He behaved, and has behaved as he acknowledged, dishonestly and criminally for [DATE_TIME]. He saw the likelihood of advantage to himself, both in terms of bail and in the sentence that he was likely to receive. You have heard that he has not yet been sentenced on matters for which he was in custody in [DATE_TIME]. The defence say if you consider the whole picture you simply cannot rely upon [PERSON]; quite unsafe to do so. The prosecution say the contents of the tapes of [DATE_TIME] can be relied on and are consistent with what [PERSON] says [the applicant] had said to him previously, before he, [PERSON], was wired up. Of course tapes of ... conversations cannot possibly constitute any independent confirmation of what [PERSON] says about what [the applicant] had said to him previously, because, and you will understand the logic of that, the information is all coming from one source, namely H. and the witness cannot strengthen his own evidence essentially by repetition. So, ladies and gentlemen, at [DATE_TIME] how do you regard [PERSON]? Was he or may he have been lying, or are you sure that he was telling the truth? If you are sure, for example, in relation to things said on the tapes of [DATE_TIME] or other aspects of H.'s evidence that his evidence is true, that [the applicant] did say a number of things, what do those things mean? Do they point to his guilt, to his presence at Kwik-Save on [DATE_TIME], or are they capable of meaning something else? ...”

The judge also directed the jury concerning the possible drawing of inferences from the applicant's silence in police interview on 28 and [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME], pursuant to section 34 of the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act [DATE_TIME]. He reminded the jury that the defence had contended that the applicant's silence had been adopted on legal advice because of the view that oppressive interrogation techniques were being used.

On [DATE_TIME], after the jury had deliberated for a total of twenty-one and [DATE_TIME], the applicant was convicted of murder before the Crown Court at Manchester by a majority of ten to two and sentenced to life imprisonment. The applicant thereafter lodged a notice of appeal, asserting, inter alia, that the judge ought to have excluded evidence of the audio- and video-recordings of his conversations with [PERSON] and J.N.S. and the evidence put forward by [PERSON] also argued that the judge had erred in his directions as to the circumstances in which the jury could draw inferences from the applicant's failure to respond to police questions in interviews of 28 and 29 June, when the police strategy was to “spook” the applicant into a state of garrulousness when he returned to prison, where he had a conversation with [PERSON] [DATE_TIME] he was refused leave to appeal against his conviction by a single judge. His renewed application was refused by the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) on [DATE_TIME], after a hearing at which he was represented by leading counsel. In the court's judgment of that date, Lord Justice [PERSON] found that the trial judge gave a very careful and impeccable ruling as regards the admissibility of the tapes and evidence put forward by [PERSON] and that he had considered all the matters which he should have considered and had not considered any matter which he ought not to have considered. There was no basis for holding that the exercise of his discretion had been so flawed that the Court of Appeal should intervene. In so far as the applicant complained that the judge should have warned the jury not to take into account the applicant's failure to answer police questioning in the light of the police strategy to “spook” him, Lord Justice [PERSON] found that the judge had given an entirely appropriate direction to the jury in the circumstances of the case.

The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 10 and 6 § 1 of the Convention.

test_texts:
PROCEDURE

The case originated in an application (no. 18753/04) against [LOCATION] lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a [NRP] national, Mr [PERSON] (“the applicant”), on [DATE_TIME].

The applicant was represented by Mrs [PERSON] Demirdaş, a lawyer practising in Tunceli. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent.

The applicant alleged, in particular, that a factual error made by the Court of Cassation had infringed his right of access to court, in violation of Article 6 of the Convention.

On [DATE_TIME] the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3 of the Convention).

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

The applicant was born in [DATE_TIME] and lives in [LOCATION].

On [DATE_TIME] the General Directorate of National Roads and Highways (hereinafter “the Directorate”) expropriated 4,309 square metres of the applicant’s land in Tunceli. The expropriation decision was communicated to the applicant on [DATE_TIME]. According to the domestic procedure, the applicant had [DATE_TIME], which began [DATE_TIME] after the decision was communicated to him, to ask for an increase in the amount of compensation.

On [DATE_TIME] a certain Mr [PERSON], who had been authorised by the applicant to appoint a lawyer for him, had a power of attorney drawn up at a notary public, appointing Mrs [PERSON] Demirdaş as legal counsel to represent the applicant.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant, with the assistance of his lawyer Mrs [PERSON], brought an action before the Tunceli Civil Court (hereinafter the “Tunceli Court”), seeking increased compensation. Mrs [PERSON] requested the court to accept the case despite the expiry of the statutory time-limit on [DATE_TIME], as she had had health problems preventing her lodging the case earlier.

On [DATE_TIME] the Tunceli Court asked the Forensic Medicine Institute in [LOCATION] to clarify whether Mrs [PERSON] had had health problems at the relevant time and whether those problems had been of a nature to render it impossible for her to come to the court house and lodge the applicant’s case within the statutory time-limit.

On [DATE_TIME] the [LOCATION] branch of the Forensic Medicine Institute forwarded to the Tunceli Court a number of medical reports, confirming that Mrs [PERSON] had been ill [DATE_TIME] and [DATE_TIME] and had thus been unable to lodge the case within the statutory time-limit.

The Tunceli Court accepted the medical report and began examining the merits of the case. In the course of the proceedings it had regard to the zone plan, the expropriation documentation, two principal and two additional expert reports, and awarded the applicant additional compensation on [DATE_TIME]. The Directorate appealed.

On [DATE_TIME] the Court of Cassation quashed the decision, quoting the applicant’s name, instead of that of his representative, as the person who had been ill. The Court of Cassation stated that the applicant had given a power of attorney to [PERSON] Demirdaş so that, even if he had been ill, Mrs [PERSON] could have lodged the claim on his behalf within the statutory time-limit. The Court of Cassation consequently held that the case had been time-barred on [DATE_TIME].

In an application for rectification Mrs [PERSON] argued that it was she who had been ill, not her client. The Court of Cassation had therefore made a factual error which should be rectified.

On [DATE_TIME], the Court of Cassation held that “amending the factual error would not affect the outcome”, and dismissed the rectification request.

On [DATE_TIME] the Tunceli Court concurred with the Court of Cassation’s decision and dismissed the case. On [DATE_TIME] the Court of Cassation upheld the final ruling.

PROCEDURE

The applicant was represented by Mr [PERSON], a lawyer practising in [PERSON] (Tarragona). The Spanish Government (“the Government”) were initially represented by their Agent, Mr [PERSON], and later by their Agent, Mr [PERSON].

The applicant complained under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of the Convention that he had not been given a proper and adequate opportunity, during either the investigative stage or the hearing, to challenge and question the victim, the sole witness against him in relation to all the crimes for which he had been convicted, with the exception of the forgery of official documents.

On [DATE_TIME] the application was communicated to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1).

On [DATE_TIME] the Court informed the Albanian Government of their right under Article 36 § 1 of the Convention to intervene in the proceedings. The Albanian Government did not inform the Court of their wish to intervene.

THE FACTS

I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

The applicant, Mr [PERSON], was born in [DATE_TIME] and is currently serving a term of imprisonment in the [NRP] prison of [PERSON] in [LOCATION] ([LOCATION]).

On [DATE_TIME], following reports to the police made by [PERSON], the applicant’s former partner and the mother of his son, the applicant was arrested at [LOCATION] ([LOCATION]) and taken to a police station where he was informed of his right to appoint private legal counsel or, alternatively, to be provided with an officially appointed lawyer. The applicant opted for the latter.

Investigating judge no. 5 of Gavà ([LOCATION]) instituted a pre-trial investigation into allegations that the applicant had committed several serious offences of bodily harm, abduction and rape of [PERSON] On [DATE_TIME] the applicant was brought before the investigating judge to be questioned about the offences of which he had been accused. He was accompanied by his officially appointed lawyer. The applicant was first informed by the judge of his right to appoint private legal counsel. He expressly appointed as private counsel the lawyer who had been officially assigned to him, who assisted him during his examination by the investigating judge. On [DATE_TIME] the applicant was questioned again by the judge, in the presence of his counsel.

On [DATE_TIME] N. testified before the investigating judge; the applicant’s counsel failed to attend without providing a justification. [PERSON] confirmed the statement she had made to the police with the addition of some further details. This statement was written up and added to the case file. From the documents submitted it does not appear that the applicant instituted any liability proceedings against his counsel for negligence.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant dismissed his counsel and personally appointed another one, who took over his defence.

The hearing before the Barcelona Audiencia Provincial took place on [DATE_TIME]. [PERSON] attended the hearing after undergoing a psychological diagnosis which established her suitability to testify in court. She had started to answer the questions posed by the public prosecutor when her statement had to be interrupted, as she was said to be suffering from post‑traumatic stress symptoms that were hindering her from testifying. Those symptoms were medically confirmed after the hearing. As a consequence, she could not be cross-examined by the public prosecutor, the private prosecutor or the applicant’s counsel. The court had already adjourned the hearing once before, following a similar reaction on the part of [PERSON] As a consequence, it had provided her with psychological assistance before and during the hearing on [DATE_TIME] to allow for her full examination, but to no avail. At the time of the suspension [of the proceedings] the victim was presenting obvious post-traumatic stress symptoms, which were hampering her memory and wrecked her capacity to express herself. The court’s final decision [i.e. to suspend the witness‑victim’s examination and replace it with the reading out of the statements she had made to the police and the investigating judge] was not arbitrary, but was made in the light of what had happened at a prior hearing which had also had to be suspended – for the same reason – and at which the psychological treatment of the victim had been ordered, the court’s perception having been confirmed by a valuable therapeutic procedure, which nonetheless did not result in the victim overcoming her incapacity. Both the persistence in the witness’s condition during the new hearing and the failure of the therapeutic procedure, which did not lead the court to feel optimistic in the short run (the proceedings concerning an accused person in prison on remand), justified the final decision to declare the victim’s examination impracticable. The court had previously attempted – perhaps to the point of excess – to exhaust all remedies to obtain her statement. It had made use of all the psychological support that the presence of officials from the victims’ service could provide to the witness, relaxation exercises during the trial, suspensions and recesses. It had also attempted, – as a kind of safety valve – to fragment her account regarding the most violent events and to redirect her attention to other events that had been less emotionally intense. The efforts were fruitless, however, and the witness’s resolved will to collaborate was prevented by one of the most horrific cases of psychological annihilation of a victim that this court has ever witnessed in its long professional experience. The witness rightly started her statement by giving a detailed description of the evolution of her relationship with the accused, the process of rupture and how their personal relations had developed in its aftermath in the light of their common child. Her determination began to weaken when, with slightly shaking hands, she began to describe the assaults she had suffered on [DATE_TIME]. The shaking later developed into an uncontrollable trembling of her mouth and her entire body as soon as she started to describe the specific aggressions she had been subjected to. Whether she was encouraged to stand up, sit down, drink water or have her hands held, nothing was of the slightest help to calm her down. Only continuous breaks and recesses and an excessive effort on her part enabled her to make, in [DATE_TIME], some progress in her statement, which came to a dramatic end as she was telling the court about the episode of a cold-water bath with which she had been tortured. Her testimony essentially corroborated her pre-trial statement and proved the authenticity of her post-traumatic stress, which was later confirmed by an expert report. The continuation of the witness’s examination would have been incompatible with Article 8 § 4 of the Protection of Victims Statute approved by a European Union Framework Decision of [DATE_TIME], which states that ‘Each Member State shall ensure that, where there is a need to protect a victim - particularly those most vulnerable - from the effects of giving evidence in open court, victims may, following a decision taken by the court, be entitled to testify in a manner which will enable this objective to be achieved, by any appropriate means compatible with its basic legal principles’.”

As an alternative to having [PERSON] questioned by the parties, the Barcelona Audiencia Provincial ordered that the statements which had been taken from her during the investigation stage of the proceedings be read out. The applicant gave his alternative account of the facts.

On [DATE_TIME] the Barcelona Audiencia Provincial delivered its judgment. Upon leaving the apartment, he had twice knocked a car belonging to J., a close male friend of [PERSON], causing damage to the vehicle. They had culminated in her hands and feet being tied, being immersed in icy water, thrown on a bed and raped vaginally and anally. Afterwards she had been obliged to phone J. and give him the address to which he should bring the child. At the time of the arranged meeting, the applicant had left the apartment for a short time in which [PERSON] had been given dry clothes by a hooded man who had left the room before the applicant had come back with [PERSON] and the child. They had remained together in the apartment for [DATE_TIME], after which the applicant had let them go under death threats. Lastly, the court found that, when the applicant had been arrested at [LOCATION] ([LOCATION]), he had been carrying false identification documents.

The applicant was sentenced as the principal offender for: (i) making very serious threats to [PERSON], to [DATE_TIME] imprisonment; (ii) breaking and entering into N.’s home using violence and coercion, to [DATE_TIME] imprisonment and a fine of [DATE_TIME] minimum income with a [DATE_TIME] fee of 12 euros (EUR); (iii) causing minor bodily injuries to [PERSON], to [DATE_TIME] house arrest; (iii) causing minor bodily injuries to J., to [DATE_TIME] house arrest; (iv) [PERSON]’s kidnapping under threat, with the aggravating factor of family ties, to [DATE_TIME] imprisonment; (v) J.’s kidnapping, to [DATE_TIME] imprisonment; (vi) a crime against [PERSON]’s moral integrity with the aggravating factor of family ties, to [DATE_TIME] imprisonment; (vii) [PERSON]’s rape with the aggravating factor of family ties, to [DATE_TIME] imprisonment; and (viii) forgery of official documents, to [DATE_TIME] imprisonment and a fine of [DATE_TIME] minimum income with a [DATE_TIME] fee of EUR 12. He was also fined EUR 30,525 for damages.

For the applicant’s above-mentioned conviction the Audiencia Provincial relied mainly on the alleged victim’s pre-trial statements, which had been admitted as evidence and read out at the hearing. The credibility of her testimony was enhanced by the weakness of the applicant’s statement. The trial court also relied on other evidence. In his statement the applicant had admitted the veracity of the details in [PERSON]’s account that did not have or had minor criminal implications, such as her changing into clothes belonging to him during her kidnapping, the damage inflicted on J.’s car, and the fact that [PERSON] had eventually brought him his child at an absolutely inappropriate time. It also relied on J.’s statement at the hearing; the contradictions of a hearsay witness for the defence as to the way in which the applicant had entered N.’s apartment; a medical report stating that the bodily injuries presented by [PERSON] were fully consistent with the aggressions she had reported; the forensic medical opinion that the bodily injuries presented by the victim [DATE_TIME] after the facts were temporarily and causally consistent with the aggressions reported; the expert opinion that [PERSON] was suffering from a post-traumatic stress disorder consistent with the facts reported; and, lastly, the court’s direct assessment of N.’s psychological inability to relive the facts that she had described – albeit only in part – at the hearing sufficiently accurately and coherently to evoke clearly what had actually happened. The court further considered that the reliability of N.’s statement had been enhanced when confronted with the applicant’s implausible statement.

The Supreme Court reduced the penalty imposed on the applicant in respect of kidnapping to bring it into line with the prosecutor’s submissions, lessened the classification of the offence of making threats and reduced the penalty imposed on the applicant in that respect, and acquitted him of the crime against moral integrity because, in the instant case, this crime could be considered to come under the offence of rape. The remainder of the Audiencia Provincial’s judgment was upheld.

The Supreme Court maintained that the applicant’s rights to examine witnesses against him and to be presumed innocent had not been infringed by the trial court’s decision to admit [PERSON]’s pre-trial statements as evidence in the proceedings. Firstly, the Audiencia Provincial had decided not to pursue N.’s cross-examination only once it had become clear that it would not be feasible to attempt to proceed. The trial court had first tried to resolve the problem by staying the hearing and ordering a medical examination of the witness with a view to excluding any possibility of feigning on her part and to adequately assess her apparent inability to give a statement before the court.When the same difficulties had recurred at the final hearing, the trial court had ordered that [PERSON] should be provided with medical support with a view to obtaining a direct testimony, which in the end proved impossible despite the efforts in that regard. Secondly, although the general rule was that witnesses should always be available for cross-examination at a hearing, the law permitted that pre-trial statements could be read out in the courtroom as an alternative when a witness’s testimony could not be produced owing to circumstances beyond the parties’ control, such as a physical or psychological impediment on the part of the witness to give a statement at the hearing, provided that the alleged impediment had been tested. Thirdly, the applicant’s counsel had been duly summoned to the judicial interview with [PERSON] during the investigative stage of the proceedings, but had failed to attend without providing a justification.

The Supreme Court contended that it had repeatedly stressed that trial courts should take special care in assessing victims’ statements when they were the sole direct evidence against the accused. It further reiterated its advice that trial courts should identify further evidence to corroborate those statements so that they may assess them objectively. The trial courts should be satisfied that those statements have not been capriciously changed during the proceedings and that there are no prior relations between the victims and the accused that could put into question the credibility of their statement. The Supreme Court added that the delay with which [PERSON] had reported the facts to the police could be explained by her fear and by the fact that she had had a child with the applicant. It further contended that it did not find in [PERSON]’s statement any alteration or substantial change which could be deemed as rendering it inconsistent and thus weakening its validity.

The applicant lodged an amparo appeal with the Constitutional Court. In a decision served on [DATE_TIME], the appeal was declared inadmissible for being devoid of any constitutional content.

On [DATE_TIME] the Chrzanów District Court ([PERSON]) gave a decision (postanowienie) declaring that, under the will of [PERSON] (the applicant’s mother-in-law), her estate be inherited by her three daughters [LOCATION], [NRP] and [PERSON] (the applicant’s wife) and by her granddaughter ([PERSON]). On [DATE_TIME] [LOCATION] (Sąd Rejonowy) declared that the applicant had inherited the estate of his late wife.

1. Facts prior to 1 [DATE_TIME]

On [DATE_TIME] [LOCATION], [NRP] and [PERSON] (“the petitioners”) filed with the Kraków District Court ([LOCATION]) an application for distribution of the estate of [PERSON] The estate consisted of three plots of land and a house and had so far been held in individual shares. The applicant was a party to these proceedings as a successor to his wife.

On [DATE_TIME] the Kraków District Court gave a decision (postanowienie) distributing the estate. Upon the applicant’s appeal, on [DATE_TIME] the Kraków Regional Court ([PERSON]) partly amended the first-instance decision.

On [DATE_TIME], on an extraordinary appeal lodged by the Minister of Justice, the Supreme Court ([PERSON]) set aside both above decisions and remitted the case to the court of first instance.

On [DATE_TIME] the District Court gave a decision. On [DATE_TIME] the Regional Court quashed that decision and remitted the case. On [DATE_TIME] the District Court gave a subsequent decision. On [DATE_TIME] the Regional Court set it aside.

On [DATE_TIME] the District Court gave a decision. On [DATE_TIME] the Regional Court dismissed the applicant’s further appeal against that decision.

On [DATE_TIME], on an extraordinary appeal lodged by the Minister of Justice, the Supreme Court partly quashed the decisions of both lower courts, and remitted the case to the District Court. On [DATE_TIME] the decision of the District Court of [DATE_TIME], in respect of the manner in which the estate was distributed, became final. The subsequent proceedings concerned solely the amount of payments for the respective shares in the estate.

Prior to 1 [DATE_TIME] there were 38 hearings held in the case before the District Court, the Regional Court and the Supreme Court. During that period the courts dealing with the case heard evidence from at least fifteen witnesses and five experts. There were eleven expert reports submitted to the courts and five inspections of the site took place. On five occasions the applicant challenged the judges dealing with the case which resulted in a delay of [DATE_TIME]. The proceedings were stayed on two occasions (on [DATE_TIME] by the Supreme Court and on [DATE_TIME] by the District Court) which resulted in a delay of [DATE_TIME].

2. Facts after [DATE_TIME]

On [DATE_TIME] the District Court ordered that a fresh report from expert [PERSON] be obtained. On [DATE_TIME] the applicant challenged that expert and requested the court to obtain an additional report from expert A.S.

On [DATE_TIME] expert [PERSON] submitted his report to the District Court. There were certain difficulties in the preparation of that report which were caused by the parties. On [DATE_TIME] the applicant again requested the court to obtain a report from another expert.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant challenged the presiding judge. On [DATE_TIME] the District Court dismissed that challenge as unfounded.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant requested the court to issue an interim order and to enter a warning in the land register about the proceedings related to the estate.

On [DATE_TIME] the petitioners submitted their observations on the expert report. On [DATE_TIME] the applicant submitted his observations. He also requested the court to obtain a report from another expert. On [DATE_TIME] the applicant filed further pleadings with the court.

On [DATE_TIME] the District Court held a hearing. It dismissed the applicant’s request of [DATE_TIME]. On [DATE_TIME] the applicant asked the court to call a witness and submitted his further observations on the expert report.

On [DATE_TIME] expert [PERSON] submitted to the court yet another report. On [DATE_TIME] the petitioners submitted their observations on that report. In principle, they agreed with its conclusions but requested that a further supplementary report be prepared.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant requested the court to issue an interim order. The District Court set a hearing for [DATE_TIME]. It was adjourned to [DATE_TIME] at the petitioners’ request. On [DATE_TIME] the applicant challenged the presiding judge.

On [DATE_TIME] the court held a hearing and heard the expert. On [DATE_TIME] the court dismissed the applicant’s request of [DATE_TIME]. On [DATE_TIME] the expert submitted his reply to the applicant’s observations on his report.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant appealed against the decision of [DATE_TIME]. On [DATE_TIME] the applicant rectified procedural defects in his appeal and paid the fee due for lodging the appeal. On [DATE_TIME] the Kraków Regional Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal. On [DATE_TIME] the case file was received at the registry of the District Court.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant filed with the court his reply to the submissions of the expert of [DATE_TIME]. On [DATE_TIME] the court held a hearing and heard evidence from two witnesses and the expert [PERSON]

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant asked the court to obtain a report from another expert. On [DATE_TIME] the applicant asked the court to issue an interim order to secure his claims in the proceedings. On [DATE_TIME] the court held a hearing. It refused the applicant’s request for an interim order and invited the parties to settle the case. On the same date, on the joint request of the parties, the court stayed the proceedings.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant asked the court that the proceedings be resumed as he disagreed with the amount of payment proposed to him by other petitioners (within the framework of the settlement). On [DATE_TIME] the court refused.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant again asked the court – this time successfully – to resume the proceedings. On [DATE_TIME] the court held a hearing. It heard evidence from two witnesses and imposed a fine on another witness who did not appear at the hearing. A hearing fixed for [DATE_TIME] was adjourned at the petitioners’ request.

At the hearing held on [DATE_TIME] the court heard evidence from one witness. The court gave all petitioners a time-limit of [DATE_TIME] for the submission of their proposals concerning re-evaluation of items included in the expert report.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant asked the court to obtain a report from another expert. The court granted that request and attempted to find an expert. Two experts refused to prepare a report. On [DATE_TIME] unspecified date expert [PERSON] agreed to prepare a report.

On [DATE_TIME] expert [PERSON] submitted his report to the court. On [DATE_TIME] the petitioners contested the report.

On [DATE_TIME] the court ordered expert [PERSON] to prepare a supplementary report, taking into account the market value of the estate. On [DATE_TIME] the expert replied that he was not able to do so. On [DATE_TIME] the court ordered yet another expert, [PERSON], to prepare a report in order to determine the market value of the estate (taking as the starting point 26 [DATE_TIME], the date on which the court had decided to grant the estate to S.Z.).

On [DATE_TIME] the court, in the presence of the expert and the petitioners, held a view of the estate. On [DATE_TIME] the expert submitted his report. On [DATE_TIME] the petitioners requested the court to reschedule a hearing fixed for [DATE_TIME]. On [DATE_TIME] the court refused that request.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant submitted his observations on the expert report, in which he objected to its findings. On [DATE_TIME] the applicant requested the court to summon expert [PERSON] in order to explain the differences in the value of the estate between the two expert reports.

On [DATE_TIME] the court held a hearing. The court closed the examination of the case. On [DATE_TIME] the applicant requested the court to obtain yet another expert report.

On [DATE_TIME] the District Court gave a decision and ordered S.Z. to pay off the applicant’s share in the estate. It dismissed the applicant’s claim for the maintenance expenses and for the house to be divided because these issues had already been determined in the decision of [DATE_TIME] ([PERSON]). The court based its decision exclusively on the report of [DATE_TIME] prepared by expert [PERSON], which assessed the market value of the estate. It regarded the reports prepared by experts [PERSON] and J.W. outdated. In respect of the report prepared by expert [PERSON] the court considered that it should not have been taken into account.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant appealed and asked the court to exempt him from a fee due for lodging an appeal. On [DATE_TIME] the petitioners filed their appeals. On [DATE_TIME] the District Court decided to exempt the applicant from the appeal fee.

On [DATE_TIME] the case file was transferred to the Regional Court. On [DATE_TIME] the applicant challenged the impartiality of two judges of that court. On [DATE_TIME] the Regional Court held a hearing. It was adjourned until [DATE_TIME] due to the absence of a witness. On the latter date the court heard evidence from a witness and expert [PERSON] The court closed examination of the case and adjourned delivery of a decision until [DATE_TIME]. On [DATE_TIME] the court dismissed the applicant’s challenge of [DATE_TIME]. On [DATE_TIME] the Regional Court dismissed both appeals.

On [DATE_TIME] the applicant filed a notice of cassation appeal. On [DATE_TIME] he requested the Regional Court to be exempted from a court fee due for lodging a cassation appeal. On [DATE_TIME] the applicant lodged his cassation appeal. On [DATE_TIME] the Regional Court refused the applicant’s request for exemption from the fee. On [DATE_TIME] the applicant paid the fee himself.

On [DATE_TIME] the Supreme Court heard, and dismissed the applicant’s cassation appeal.

train_texts: The case was referred to the Court, in accordance with the provisions applicable prior to the entry into force of Protocol No. 11 to the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The case originated in an application (no. 24876/94) against [LOCATION] lodged with the Commission under former Article 25 of the Convention by two [NRP] nationals. The applicants alleged that planning and enforcement measures taken against them in respect of their occupation of their land in their caravans violated their right to respect for home, family life and private life. The Commission declared the application admissible on [DATE_TIME]. The Grand Chamber determined that the case should be decided by the Grand Chamber. The applicants and the Government each filed a memorial. Third-party comments were also received from the European Roma Rights Centre. The applicants are gypsies by birth and live in and around the Borough of Maidstone. There remained few stopping places upon which they could lawfully park their caravan whilst travelling in the area and they faced the threat of continual eviction. They wished for their children to be brought up in a safe place. The Government were given leave by the President to intervene in the written procedure. The case was heard by the Grand Chamber and the Court heard addresses by Mr [PERSON] and Mr [DATE_TIME]. The applicants were refused a place on any local authorised site. They camped outside one official site for [DATE_TIME] hoping to be offered a plot. No place was offered and court proceedings were brought against them by the Borough to secure their eviction from the land. The Government stated that the Borough has no knowledge or record of any request by the applicants for a pitch. The applicants disputed that they owed any rent and suggested that the borough has mistaken them for the tenants of a different flat, there being some confusion as to the addresses involved. The application was denied and an enforcement notice was issued requiring discontinuance of the unauthorised use of the site. A public enquiry was held by way of appeal against the refusal of planning permission. The appeal was dismissed. The Inspector accepted that the applicants were gypsies for whom conventional residence in permanent accommodation would lead to illness and problems of adjustment. He found however that the development on a site, well outside built-up areas, was clearly visible and would constitute a significant intrusion into the attractive rural surroundings. The inspector did not find the granting of permission for caravans for two gypsy families some 300-400 metres away along the same road could be regarded as a material difference. “On the contrary, in my opinion three gypsy caravan sites within some 600 m of the length of [LOCATION] would amount to an overconcentration of caravan sites in these rural surroundings” Inspector: "I accept that the family have a pressing local need for a caravan site" Kent County Council support the provision of private sites. Government policy. should be a flexible attitude to such planning applications. Well-run gypsy sites, once established, seldom give cause for serious complaints. ‘Designated’ authorities like Maidstone may still need to make extra provision in their area if the demand for gypsy accommodation increases. There are still gypsy families parked on unauthorised sites in the [LOCATION] area, including [the applicants]… No new gypsy. sites have been opened in [ LOCATION] since [DATE_TIME]. The applicants were convicted for breach of enforcement notices and ordered to pay GBP 275 each as a fine and contribute GBP 25 to the Borough’s costs. They had terminated their council tenancy to move onto land not permitted for residential use contrary to the advice of the Housing and Planning Departments. The applicants were recorded as stating that they would not accept a place on an official site and would only accept temporary accommodation in their own caravan, which the Borough could not provide. According to the Government, in [DATE_TIME], the applicants applied to the borough for housing on the grounds of homelessness. The Borough agreed to re-register them as homeless on condition that they paid their arrears of rent for the council tenancy. Borough took the decision to seek an injunction in the High Court restraining the applicants from stationing their caravan on their land. On [DATE_TIME], the applicants left their land and travelled to Whitstable, Kent close to where some of the second applicant’s family had stationed their caravans. On the site there was no sanitation or electricity and there was an infestation of rats. The applicants were informed, the Government stated, of vacant plots on council and private gypsy sites in the county. One site which they visited at Aylesford was infested with rats and a dangerous place for children. The Government stated that the applicants’ names were placed on the waiting list at [Dates] but they removed their names from that list. The applicants bought a touring caravan, which they stationed on the land of the second applicant’s brother. They took every opportunity they could to travel in the traditional style during school holidays, attending traditional gypsy fairs to continue horse trading activities and for the first applicant to find work landscaping and tree-felling. The applicants suffered headaches, anxiety, claustrophobia and depression requiring them to seek medical treatment. The Department of the Environment statistics for gypsy caravan sites for [DATE_TIME] indicated that in the [LOCATION] area there were two local authority sites comprising 34 pitches. In addition, there were 96 caravans on authorised private sites and eight [NRP] on unauthorised sites, two of which were tolerated by the local authority. Number of unauthorised encampments remained at eight. The number of public authorised sites had decreased from 34 to 32. Number of authorised private sites decreased from 96 to 89.
